Hiraṇyakeśi Dharmasūtras
------------------------------------------
Secondary scriptures like the smṛtis, आगमस् and पुराणस्, have a say even today in the life of the Hindus. The धर्मसूत्रस् which are part of these secondary scriptures, are quite ancient.
The Hiraṇyakeśi Dharmasūtras which forms an integral part of a bigger work, the Hiraṇyakeśi Kalpasūtras (praśnas 26 and 27), is not considered as an independent work since it borrows profusely from the Āpastamba Dharmasūtras.
It belongs to the Taittirīya branch of Yajurveda. There is a commentary called Ujjvalā by महादेव Dīkṣita.
The work must have been composed much earlier than A.

.
The contents of this work are practically the same as those of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtras.
See ĀPASTAMBA.

Hiraṇyagarbha
(‘golden egg’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Advaita Vedānta he is the second aspect of ब्रह्मन्, the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, associated with अज्ञान or nescience, after ईश्वर. He is connected with the totality of the sūkṣmaśarīras or subtle bodies in च्रेअतिओन्, permeating them like the thread passing through the beads. Hence the name ‘Sūtrātman’. He is also called ‘prāṇa,’ being the subtle principle of life. The unmanifested, seed-state of च्रेअतिओन् is compared to a golden egg. Since he keeps it in his womb as it were, before manifesting it, he is called ‘Hiraṇyagarbha’ (‘golden egg’). He has the three powers of will, knowledge and action, known as इच्छाशक्ति, ज्ञानशक्ति and क्रियाशक्ति.

Hiraṇyakaśipu
(‘one who has covered himself with gold’, ‘the greedy one’)
------------------------------------------
Jaya and विजय, the gate-keepers of वैकुण्ठ (the abode of विष्णु) were once cursed by the sages सनक, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra and Sanatsujāta, to be born as राक्षसस् (demons). The curse was to be effective for three births only.
They were hence born as हिरण्याक्ष and हिरण्यकशिपु in the कृतयुग, as रावण and कुम्भकर्ण in the Tretā-yuga, and as शिशुपाल and Dantavaktra in the द्वापरयुग. In all the three births they were killed by Lord विष्णु in his incarnations as Varāha, नरसिṁह, राम and कृष्ण.
Hiraṇyakaśipu, the son of कश्यप and दिति, was enraged by the killing of his twin-brother हिरण्याक्ष at the hands of विष्णु. He performed severe austerities, pleased the god ब्रह्मा and secured several boons from him. Emboldened by these, he conquered the gods in हेअवेन् and started harassing one and all.
He had four sons, of whom प्रह्लाद (the famous child-devotee) was the eldest. Since this boy was deeply devoted to विष्णु, हिरण्यकशिपु tried his level best, first to ‘reform’ him and then to liquidate him. But by Lord विष्णु’s grace and protection the boy remained unharmed! Finally हिरण्यकशिपु was killed by the lord in the form of नरसिṁह (man-lion), thus ridding the world, of an incorrigible tyrant.

Hiraṇyagarbha Sūkta
------------------------------------------
The sūktas from the Ṛgveda are widely used in the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् either as prayers or as mantras for the performance of appropriate rituals. One such सूक्त used in पशुबन्ध sacrifices is the Hiraṇyagarbha Sūkta.
Though used as a part of Vedic ritual, this सूक्त has a profound philosophical import.
Originally it appears in the Ṛgveda (10.121). It is repeated in the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (

) of Yajurveda and the Paippalāda Saṁhitā (4.2) of the Atharva-veda with slight changes.
This सूक्त has ten ṛks or stanza each of which ends with the words, ‘kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema.’
The word ‘ka’ and its dative case, ‘kasmai,’ repeated in every stanza, has rather posed a problem of interpretation. The simplest meanings are, ‘who’ and ‘to whom’. However, this direct meaning does not allow grammatically proper syntactical connection. Hence commentators have struggled to give other interpretations.
Depending on an anecdote in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (12.21) सायण (14th century), the well-known commentator of the वेदस्, interprets the word ‘ka’ as a name of प्रजापति (one of the aspects of God) the creator of the world.
According to another interpretation ‘ka’ means ‘bliss’.
Hence the sentence would mean, ‘We offer the oblations unto God, the creator, who is bliss-personified.’
A brief summary of the सूक्त can now be given:
Hiraṇyagarbha (God the creator in whom the whole world existed in a seed-form like a golden egg) alone existed in the beginning. He created the world and was its supreme monarch. It was he who was responsible for supporting हेअवेन् and earth. Again, it was he who gave strength to all the living beings including the gods, who have been obeying his commands. The हिमालयस्, the oceans and the rivers are reflecting his glory. If the earth and हेअवेन् have been firmly established in their places, if the sun and the rainbearing clouds are performing their duties regularly, it is because of him only.
This is the gist of the first seven verses.
The eighth verse indicates that primeval waters existed before च्रेअतिओन् and प्रजापति or हिरण्यगर्भ was its witness.
The next verse is a prayer to him so that he does not trouble the votaries.
The last, the tenth, verse praises him as the only one capable of creating the world and prays to him for granting or fulfilling the desires of the devotes who are offering this prayer.
